newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Analysts seek clues to Novartis progress.
newsitem.headline: Analysts seek clues to Novartis progress.

text.p: Analysts will be looking for news on Novartis AG's post-merger progress when the Swiss pharmaceuticals giant formed last year by the marriage of Ciba-Geigy and Sandoz reports its 1996 results on Tuesday.
The numbers are unlikely to contain surprises, analysts said, so the focus will be on projections for the way ahead.
"What will be important are the adjectives used to describe the near future and any information on the merger process," said Union Bancaire Privee analyst Romain Pasche.
The newly formed group has been one of the favourites on the Swiss share market since the two companies made their merger plans known last March. The group was officially formed on January 1.
But management has warned markets recently that, excluding one-off merger-related income and expenses, 1996 net income was likely to be approximately at the same level as in 1995.
Nonetheless, analysts and investors in general see great things ahead for the company after integration of the two Swiss groups is complete.
Novartis reported in January that its 1996 sales rose to 36.23 billion Swiss francs from 35.94 billion. The combined net income of the two groups for 1995 was 4.2 billion francs.

But given the changes being made in the new company, including the recent spin-off of Ciba's specialty chemical operations earlier this month, analysts will be looking to see how well the integration of the two companies is progressing.
"Comparisons with 1995 will be difficult to make. We really just want a base from which we can start," Pasche said.
Novartis is number two in the world in health and medical nutrition and, with market share of an estimated 4.4 percent, second only to Britain's Glaxo Wellcome In pharmaceuticals.

It is among the top global players in self-medication and vision care and the world leader in crop protection. With annual research and development spending around three billion francs, the group is just about the biggest spender in the health care sector.
Novartis management has predicted it could realise 1.8 billion francs of savings due to synergies within three years, with half of that expected within the first 18 months.
Bank Julius Baer analyst Beat Alpiger predicted that some 40 to 45 percent of the annual savings target could be achieved in 1997, with the rest coming in 1998 and 1999.
"The year 1996 is not a Novartis story. The story is from 1997 onwards," said Goldman Sachs analyst Mark Tracey.
Analysts will also watch to see if a weak trend in the pharmaceuticals business inherited from Ciba shows signs of a reversal.
The results will show that Ciba had a disappointing second half of 1996, which probably extended into the start of this year, Tracey added.

Interim reports from Ciba last year showed sales of the anti-rheumatic drug Voltaren, its most successful drug, and sales of the anti-hypertension medication Lopresor were hurt by generic competition in the U.S.
U.S. Voltaren sales fell by eight percent and Lopresor sales were down 27 percent last year.
Sales of other Ciba pharma products, including Nitroderm, Estraderm and Ritalin, were also weak in the second half and its agrochemicals turnover was hit by a stronger dollar.
Novartis's shares, after some recent gains, are trading at about 21 times estimated 1998 earnings, compared to an average of some 23 percent for other major companies in the sector.
One reason for the lower ratio might be the fact that investors view Swiss companies as being less transparent than their counterparts in the U.S. or Britain, Pasche noted.

He also said that many of the group's leading products, especially on the Ciba side, are quite mature. In the short-term, analysts will therefore need to hear some good news about new products in the Novartis pipeline.
